snippet.title: Hare Krishna Maha Mantra to Sing Along, 108 Times (21 Min Kirtan That Speeds Up)
snippet.description:
The Hare Krishna maha mantra, 108 times, sung kirtan style in 21 minutes: first one voice, then call and response, then everyone with a band that keeps speeding up, and back down to a whisper. Sing along: the word being sung lights up on screen with its meaning underneath, and a mala of 108 beads fills at the top.

Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare, Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare.

What it is: the Hare Krishna maha mantra ("great mantra"), sixteen Sanskrit words from the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, sung every day in the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition and carried around the world by ISKCON since 1966. All three words are a call: Hare addresses Harā, the Lord's energy (Rādhā); Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are names of God. Say it HAH-ray, KRISH-nuh, RAH-muh.

In the tradition: Prabhupada explained it as a prayer, "O energy of the Lord, O Lord, please engage me in Your service". The Upanishad's name means "crossing over Kali": these sixteen names are said to carry you through the age of quarrel. Chanting them with others is called kirtan.

Why a repeated sound can calm you: in a 2001 BMJ study, 23 healthy adults recited "om-mani-padme-om" and the rosary; both slowed breathing to about 6 breaths a minute and made the heart-rhythm reflexes stronger (Bernardi et al.). In a 2024 study, 34 adults chanted "om" for 12 minutes and their saliva cortisol and anxiety went down (Perry, Polito & Thompson); there was no group that didn't chant. In a pilot brain scan of 12 people, chanting "om" lowered activity in emotion areas, the amygdala among them, compared with rest; saying "ssss" did not (Kalyani et al., 2011). Small studies, short effects, a few minutes at a time: calmer, not cured. None of them tested a video like this one, a whole session, studying or karma.

And if karma is real, this should clean a little of yours. The tradition says singing the names "cleans the mirror of the heart" and grows joy (Chaitanya's Shikshashtaka, verse 1). Good karma, joy, a calmer week, or all three. No promises, no cure.

Ways to use it: sing the first rounds along with the single voice and let your breath slow down; put it on while you cook or tidy; play it before a hard conversation or at the end of a long day; or keep it low while you work. Listening only is fine too.

snippet.title: Om Mani Padme Hum to Study, 1 Hour
snippet.description:
One hour of Om Mani Padme Hum to study or work by, so you can stop choosing a playlist: one mantra, a steady pulse around 100 beats a minute, a quiet band, women's voices that come and go, and seven parts so the hour does not feel like one long loop. The word being sung lights up on screen with its meaning underneath, a mala of 108 beads fills at the top, a counter shows the rounds and the clock shows the minutes left.

Oṃ Maṇi Padme Hūṃ, said the Tibetan way: Om Mani Peme Hung. It is written Padme Hūṃ and sung "Peme Hung", and that is how it is sung here.

What it is: the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteśvara (Chenrezig in Tibetan), the bodhisattva of compassion, recited, carved and spun in prayer wheels across Tibetan Buddhism. Mani means jewel and padme lotus; the Dalai Lama explains the jewel as compassion and the lotus as wisdom. A mala, the string of prayer beads, usually has 108 beads, one for each round.

In the tradition: it is chanted to call up Chenrezig's compassion for all beings. The Dalai Lama teaches that the six syllables stand for a path that unites method and wisdom, which can turn an impure body, speech and mind into those of a Buddha.

Why a repeated sound can calm you: in a 2001 BMJ study, 23 healthy adults recited "om-mani-padme-om" and the rosary; both slowed breathing to about 6 breaths a minute and made the heart-rhythm reflexes stronger (Bernardi et al.). In a 2024 study, 34 adults chanted "om" for 12 minutes and their saliva cortisol and anxiety went down (Perry, Polito & Thompson); there was no group that didn't chant. In a pilot brain scan of 12 people, chanting "om" lowered activity in emotion areas, the amygdala among them, compared with rest; saying "ssss" did not (Kalyani et al., 2011). Small studies, short effects, a few minutes at a time: calmer, not cured. None of them tested a video like this one, a whole session, studying or karma. We can't promise focus: the studies above measured calm, not concentration or grades.

And if karma is real, this should clean a little of yours. Good karma, a calmer desk, or both. No promises, no cure.

Ways to use it: as a background for studying or working; as a timer for one long block (the clock counts down the hour); to sing along on a break; or to reset the room before you start. Listening only is fine too.

In a 2024 study, 34 adults chanted "om" for 12 minutes and their saliva cortisol and anxiety went down (Perry, Polito & Thompson); there was no group that didn't chant. In a pilot brain scan of 12 people, chanting "om" lowered activity in emotion areas, the amygdala among them, compared with rest; saying "ssss" did not (Kalyani et al., 2011). Small studies, short effects, a few minutes at a time: calmer, not cured. None of them tested a video like this one, a whole session, studying or karma.

And if karma is real, this should clean a little of yours. The tradition says singing the names "cleans the mirror of the heart" and grows joy (Chaitanya's Shikshashtaka, verse 1). Good karma, joy, a calmer week, or all three. No promises, no cure.

snippet.title: The Maha Mantra Before Your Monday Inbox: Two Rounds, Then Open the Tab
snippet.description:
Cella in a flower field, swaying like the calmest one in the group, which I am. The flowers are not competition; they just have fewer opinions.

Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare, Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare.

What it is: the Hare Krishna maha mantra, sixteen names from the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, sung here at a soft, even working pace. Say it HAH-ray, KRISH-nuh, RAH-muh. (Sung in the order ISKCON chants it; the Upanishad lists Hare Rāma first.)

In the tradition: the Upanishad that names it is called Kali-Santarana, "crossing Kali", and it gives these sixteen names as the way across the age of quarrel. Hare, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are all forms of address: the mantra is a call, not a statement.

Why a sound like this may calm you: in a 2024 study, 34 adults chanted "om" for 12 minutes, aloud or in silence, and their saliva cortisol and anxiety went down (Perry, Polito & Thompson). Limit: there was no group that didn't chant, and cortisol was measured only twice. Two more lean the same way, with limits (Kalyani 2011: a pilot of 12 people; Bernardi 2001: 23 healthy adults, one session); none tested this exact mantra. Small studies, short effects: calmer, not cured.

And if karma is real, this should lighten a little of yours. If it isn't, you still gave 19 seconds to something that isn't your inbox.

Sing along, a word per beat, before you open the first tab. Then again.

Sources:
Perry, G., Polito, V., & Thompson, W. F. (2024). Exploring the physiological and psychological effects of group chanting in Australia: Reduced stress, cortisol and enhanced social connection. Journal of Religion and Health, 63(6), 4793-4815. doi:10.1007/s10943-023-01967-5
Kalyani, B. G., Venkatasubramanian, G., Arasappa, R., et al. (2011). Neurohemodynamic correlates of 'OM' chanting: A pilot functional magnetic resonance imaging study. International Journal of Yoga, 4(1), 3-6. doi:10.4103/0973-6131.78171
Bernardi, L., Sleight, P., Bandinelli, G., et al. (2001). Effect of rosary prayer and yoga mantras on autonomic cardiovascular rhythms: comparative study. BMJ, 323(7327), 1446-1449. doi:10.1136/bmj.323.7327.1446

snippet.title: Om Mani Padme Hum for the Person You're Annoyed At (It Might Be You)
snippet.description:
Cella in a bamboo forest, swaying with the stalks. Compassion for all beings. I'm a being. I checked.

Oṃ Maṇi Padme Hūṃ (sung Om Mani Peme Hung).

What it is: Om Mani Padme Hum, the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteshvara (Chenrezig), the bodhisattva of compassion. Tibetans say it Om Mani Peme Hung, the way it is sung here, soft and even, at about a walking pace.

In the tradition: Tibetans carve it on stones and write it inside prayer wheels, and the Dalai Lama asks only that you think of its meaning while you say it: the jewel is the wish to help, the lotus is wisdom, and the two go together.

Why a sound like this may calm you: in a 2001 BMJ study, 23 healthy adults recited a yoga mantra (om-mani-padme-om) and the rosary; both slowed breathing to about 6 breaths a minute, down from about 14, and strengthened the heart-rhythm reflex (Bernardi et al.). Limit: 23 healthy people, one session, and the authors are cautious about why it happens. Two more lean the same way, with limits (Perry 2024: 34 adults, no non-chanting group; Kalyani 2011: a pilot of 12 people). Small studies, short effects: calmer, not cured.

And if karma is real, this should clean a little of yours. If it isn't, you spent 28 seconds being gentle with someone, which is on the Tuesday agenda either way.

Chant it along, one syllable to a sway. Twelve rounds, then once more.

Sources:
Bernardi, L., Sleight, P., Bandinelli, G., et al. (2001). Effect of rosary prayer and yoga mantras on autonomic cardiovascular rhythms: comparative study. BMJ, 323(7327), 1446-1449. doi:10.1136/bmj.323.7327.1446

Kalyani, B. G., Venkatasubramanian, G., Arasappa, R., et al. (2011). Neurohemodynamic correlates of 'OM' chanting: A pilot functional magnetic resonance imaging study. International Journal of Yoga, 4(1), 3-6. doi:10.4103/0973-6131.78171
